title: Microsoft Fabric vs Databricks
summary: An independent comparison blog contrasting Microsoft Fabric's SaaS analytics platform with Databricks' lakehouse platform across architecture, security, BI integration, compute engines, and hybrid deployment patterns.
audience: Data platform decision-makers evaluating Fabric against Databricks for a new or migrating analytics estate.
why_it_matters: Head-to-head vendor comparisons are a common way architects triage platform choice; this piece is useful for surfacing the structural differences worth verifying against primary docs, even though its specific figures (pricing, adoption counts, release dates) are unverified third-party claims and were excluded here.
takeaways: Fabric packages Spark, SQL, Power BI, and pipelines under one SaaS capacity model, while Databricks separates compute (DBUs) from the underlying cloud VM billing.
Direct Lake is positioned as Fabric's differentiator for Power BI, avoiding an import/refresh cycle by reading Delta tables directly.
OneLake-to-Databricks interoperability is improving via mirroring/shortcut mechanisms rather than data duplication.
As of the post's writing, Direct Lake's interaction with fine-grained security models (row-level security) still had gaps worth validating before relying on it.
Fabric's Git integration for semantic models can produce merge conflicts that require manual resolution, a practitioner pain point rather than a marketing claim.

claims.text: Microsoft Fabric is architected as a single SaaS control plane where compute engines share one capacity (F-SKU) and billing surface, unlike Databricks' separately metered compute-plus-cloud-VM model.
Direct Lake is described as letting Power BI query Delta tables in OneLake directly, avoiding the import-and-refresh cycle required by traditional import-mode semantic models.
Per the post, Direct Lake's interaction with OneLake row-level security had known limitations at the time of writing, so RLS behavior should be verified before depending on it in a design.
The post describes Fabric mirroring of external platforms (including Databricks' Unity Catalog) as creating OneLake shortcuts to source data rather than copying it, avoiding duplicated storage.
Semantic models are stored as TMDL/TMSL-based definition files, and the post notes that merging concurrent changes to these files in Git can produce conflicts requiring manual resolution.
The post frames Fabric's Spark session pooling (starter pools) as reducing session cold-start time compared to provisioning a fresh cluster per job, a pattern also used by Databricks' cluster pools.

The post positions Fabric compute as remaining within Azure, contrasting it with Databricks' multi-cloud deployment model (AWS, Azure, GCP), as a consideration for organizations wanting cloud portability.
